newsitem.title: USA: GFOA says IRS yield burning rules are "unworkable".
newsitem.headline: GFOA says IRS yield burning rules are "unworkable".

text.p: The Government Finance Officers Association urged U.S. regulators to scrap its proposal telling localities how to avoid "yield burning" in the muni bond market because it is burdensome and unworkable.
In comments filed with the Internal Revenue Service, GFOA told IRS it has unfairly focused the June 26 rule on buyers of securities rather than the dealers that sell them.
The group urged IRS to better enforce existing rules that bar excessive mark-ups and require dealers to sell securities at fair and reasonable prices.
GFOA called for a "safe harbor" to protect municipalities from federal action if "qualified professionals" certify that securities were bought at fair market value.

Under such a safe harbor, dealers that sell the securities should certify they were sold at a fair and reasonable price, Catherine Spain, director of GFOA's Federal Liaison Center in Washington, said in the association's 10-page letter to IRS.
And the dealer should disclose the mark-up in the certification, Spain said.
IRS' proposed rule tells state and local governments how to invest bond proceeds so the reinvestment does not violate federal restrictions on arbitrage profits.
The rule would require an auction of at least three bids and limit fees that agents can get at .02 percent of the value of the reinvestment.
It also would bar underwriters, financial advisers and others that have a "material financial interest" in the offering from making bids to provide the reinvestment securities.
Spain said if IRS opts to take action when it detects yield burning, it should not threaten the taxability of bonds because innocent bondholders would be penalized.
It should fine the market players that are directly or indirectly responsible for excessive mark-ups, using Section 6700 of the tax code, Spain said.
"This section permits regulators to penalize parties that actually received a financial benefit as a result of the sales practice abuse and not innocent bondholders or an unwary issuer," Spain said.
She said IRS did not get enough information about the "nature, pervasiveness and cause of the yield-burning problem" before proposing its rule.
"These regulations are proposed to remedy a problem reported in the news media," Spain said.

However, regulators have provided no information on "how prevalent the problem is, what types of transactions are susceptible to yield burning, and what role issuers may have played in transactions," Spain said.
"Yield burning is an unfair sales practice, but federal actions should be based on actual violations so appropriate solutions can be designed," Spain said.
Spain's letter recounts one issuer's unsuccessful attempt to comply with IRS' proposed rule.

"Bids were solicited from nine primary dealers. Five declined to bid either because of the small amount to be invested for a short period and/or because of the certifications required to be signed," the letter says.

The bidding agent would not certify several items required by the proposed regulations, such as that the bidders did not have a material interest in the bonds or that the accepted bid was the highest yield offered, GFOA said.
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
